{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=4488", "note": "Language Log traces this to an 'invented statistic' with no verifiable original citation ever found for the 20,000/7,000 figures."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://time.com/2992051/women-talk-more-study/", "note": "Time reports a University of Pennsylvania researcher tried to trace the statistic's origin and could not confirm a legitimate study behind it."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://abcnews.com/Technology/story?id=3348076&page=1", "note": "ABC News reports the actual peer-reviewed study (Mehl et al.) found women spoke 16,215 words/day and men 15,669 words/day, a negligible, non-significant difference."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/women-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "Scientific American attributes popularization of the 20,000 vs 7,000 figures to Louann Brizendine's 'The Female Brain,' not to a rigorous study, and notes it was widely challenged."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.pimsleur.com/blog/language-ideologies-do-women-really-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "States plainly this figure 'is false but quite pervasive in popular culture' and 'is not backed by any evidence.'"}], "origin_trace": "The earliest identifiable source is Louann Brizendine's 2006 book 'The Female Brain,' which popularized the 20,000/7,000 word figures without a clear, verifiable citation; The actual peer-reviewed study on daily word counts (Mehl et al., published in Science, 2007) found women and men speak nearly the same amount (about 16,215 vs 15,669 words/day).", "reasoning": "Multiple independent sources (Language Log, Time, ABC News, Scientific American, Pimsleur) converge on the same conclusion: the 20,000 vs 7,000 word claim has no traceable legitimate scientific origin and is widely regarded as a myth. Because the figure is not merely mischaracterized but actively debunked by better data, this is not a case of framing drift but a fabricated/unsupported statistic."}
